'''Peter V. Coveney''' is a British chemist who is Professor of [[Physical Chemistry]], Honorary Professor of [[Computer Science]], and the Director of the Centre for Computational Science (CCS)<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ucl.ac.uk/computational-science/advancing-science-through-computersthe-centre-computational-science|title="The Centre for Computational Science"|date=4 May 2021 |access-date=2022-12-29}}</ref> and Associate Director of the Advanced Research Computing Centre at [[University College London|University College London (UCL)]].  He is also a Professor of Applied [[High Performance Computing]] at [[University of Amsterdam|University of Amsterdam (UvA)]] and Professor Adjunct at the [[Yale School of Medicine]], [[Yale University]]. He is a Fellow of the [[Royal Academy of Engineering]] and Member of [[Academia Europaea]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Coveney_Peter |title=Academy of Europe: Coveney Peter |publisher=Ae-info.org |date= |access-date=2021-02-13}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Royal Academy of Engineering. |url=https://raeng.org.uk/about-us/fellowship/new-fellows-2022/professor-peter-vivian-coveney-freng |access-date=2024-04-21 |website=raeng.org.uk |language=en}}</ref>
==Education==
Coveney was awarded a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] degree from  the  [[University of Oxford]] in 1985 for his work on Semiclassical methods in scattering and [[spectroscopy]].<ref name="coveneyphd">{{cite thesis|degree=DPhil|first=Peter V|last=Coveney|title=Semiclassical methods in scattering and spectroscopy|publisher=University of Oxford|date=1985|url=http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/primo_library/libweb/action/dlDisplay.do?docId=oxfaleph016235950|author-link=Peter Coveney|archive-date=20 March 2022|access-date=20 August 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220320003412/https://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/primo_library/libweb/action/dlDisplay.do?docId=oxfaleph016235950|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Career==
Coveney has held positions at [[University of Oxford]], [[Princeton University]], [[Schlumberger]] and [[Queen Mary University of London|QMUL]], and currently holds positions at [[University College London|UCL]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Peter Coveney, Professor of Physical Chemistry, Dept of Chemistry |url=https://profiles.ucl.ac.uk/3406 |access-date=2024-04-21 |website=profiles.ucl.ac.uk}}</ref> [[University of Amsterdam|UvA]] and [[Yale University|Yale]], as well as acting as a Member of several academic councils in the [[UK]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=University |first=Durham |title=Institute of Advanced Study: Professor Peter Coveney - Durham University |url=https://www.durham.ac.uk/research/institutes-and-centres/advanced-study/about-us/ |access-date=2024-04-21 |website=www.durham.ac.uk |language=en-gb}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=REF Case study search |url=https://impact.ref.ac.uk/casestudies/CaseStudy.aspx?Id=33268 |access-date=2024-04-21 |website=impact.ref.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref> and [[EU]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Amsterdam |first=Universiteit van |date=2023-10-22 |title=Prof. dr. P.V. (Peter Vivian) Coveney |url=https://www.uva.nl/en/profile/c/o/p.v.coveney/p.v.coveney.html |access-date=2024-04-21 |website=University of Amsterdam |language=en}}</ref>

===Research===
Coveney worked with [[Ilya Prigogine]] at the Free University of Brussels (1985-87) and went on to publish work with the mathematician [[Oliver Penrose]] on rigorous foundations of irreversibility and the derivation of kinetic equations based on chaotic dynamical systems.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=P.V.|last1=Coveney|title=Statistical mechanics of a large dynamical system interacting with an external time-dependent field: generalised correlation subdynamics|journal=Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and Its Applications|volume=143|date=1987|issue=3 |pages=507–534|doi=10.1016/0378-4371(87)90163-4 |bibcode=1987PhyA..143..507C }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|first1=P. V.|last1=Coveney|first2=O.|last2=Penrose|date=1992|title=On the validity of the Brussels formalism in statistical mechanics|journal=J. Phys. A: Math. Gen.|volume=25|issue=19 |page=4947|doi=10.1088/0305-4470/25/19/011 |bibcode=1992JPhA...25.4947C }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Evans|first1=Allan K.|last2=Coveney|first2=Peter V.|date=1995|title=On exponential long-time evolution in statistical mechanics|journal=Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A|volume=448|issue=1933 |pages=293–319|doi=10.1098/rspa.1995.0018 |bibcode=1995RSPSA.448..293E |s2cid=122838748 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|first1=Allan K|last1=Evans|first2=Peter V|last2=Coveney|title=On the long-time behaviour of ensembles in a model of deterministic diffusion|date=1998|journal=J. Phys. A: Math. Gen.|volume=31|issue=28 |page=5887|doi=10.1088/0305-4470/31/28/006 |bibcode=1998JPhA...31.5887E }}</ref> 

He collaborated with Jonathan Wattis on extensions and generalisations of the Becker-Döring and [[Smoluchowski coagulation equation|Smoluchowski]] equations for the kinetics of aggregation-fragmentation processes which they applied to a wide range of phenomena, from self-reproducing micelles and vesicles to a scenario for the origin of the [[RNA world]] in which they showed that self-reproducing sequences of RNA can spontaneously arise from an aqueous mixture of the RNA nucleotide bases.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Peter V.|last1=Coveney|first2=Jonathan A. D.|last2=Wattis|title=Analysis of a generalized Becker—Döring model of self-reproducing micelles|journal=Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A|volume=452|pages=2079–2102|date=1996|issue=1952 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1996.0110|bibcode=1996RSPSA.452.2079C |s2cid=95877636 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|first1=P. V.|last1=Coveney|first2=J. A. D.|last2=Wattis|title=Cluster renormalization in the Becker-Döring equations|journal=J. Phys. A: Math. Gen.|volume=32|page=7145|date=1999|issue=41 |doi=10.1088/0305-4470/32/41/308 |arxiv=cond-mat/9908402 |bibcode=1999JPhA...32.7145C |s2cid=17019314 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|first1=J. A. D.|last1=Wattis|first2=P. V.|last2=Coveney|title=The origin of the RNA world: A kinetic model|journal=J. Phys. Chem. B|volume=103|pages=4231–4250|date=1999|issue=21 |doi=10.1021/jp983159v |arxiv=adap-org/9903002 |s2cid=17792989 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wattis|first1=J. A. D.|last2=Coveney|first2=P. V.|title=Symmetry-breaking in Chiral Polymerisation|journal=Orig Life Evol Biosph|volume=35|pages=243–273|date=2005|issue=3 |doi=10.1007/s11084-005-0658-7|pmid=16228641 |arxiv=physics/0402091 |bibcode=2005OLEB...35..243W |s2cid=12451904 }}</ref>

At [[Schlumberger Cambridge Research]] (SCR), Coveney initiated new lines of research in which advanced computational methods played a central role. Some parts of this work, to develop highly scalable lattice-gas and, later, lattice-Boltzmann models of complex fluids, was done in collaboration with [[Bruce M. Boghosian]], following Schlumberger's acquisition of a [[Connection Machine]], the CM-5, from the company.{{cn|date=March 2024}}

At the same time, using methods from nonlinear dynamics, he was able to identify the rate-determining processes that enable one to design new compounds which inhibit the crystallisation of the mineral ettringite by molecular modelling.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Cellular automaton simulations of cement hydration and microstructure development|first1=D. P. |last1=Bentz|first2=P. V. |last2=Coveney|first3=E. J. |last3=Garboczi|first4=M. F. |last4=Kleyn |first5=P. E. |last5=Stutzman|journal=Modelling and Simulation in Materials Science and Engineering|year=1994 |volume=2|issue=4 |page=783|doi=10.1088/0965-0393/2/4/001 |bibcode=1994MSMSE...2..783B |s2cid=250845929 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Coveney |first1=P. V. |last2=Fletcher |first2=P. |last3=Hughes |first3=T. L. |date=1996 |title=Using Artificial Neural Networks to Predict the Quality and Performance of Oil-Field Cements |journal=AI Magazine |volume=17 |issue=4 |page=41 |doi=10.1609/aimag.v17i4.1239}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Scott |first1=D. J. |last2=Coveney |first2=P. V. |last3=Kilner |first3=J. A. |last4=Rossiny |first4=J. C. H. |last5=Alford |first5=N. M. N. |year=2007 |title=Prediction of the functional properties of ceramic materials from composition using artificial neural networks |journal=Journal of the European Ceramic Society |volume=27 |issue=16 |pages=4425–4435 |arxiv=cond-mat/0703210 |doi=10.1016/j.jeurceramsoc.2007.02.212 |s2cid=16162179}}</ref>

From 2006, Coveney moved away from studying oilfield fluids to investigate blood flow in the human body, including the brain. Working with a PhD student, Marco Mazzeo, he developed a new code, named HemeLB, which simulates blood flow in the complex geometries of the human vasculature, as derived from a variety of medical imaging modalities.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=M. D. |last1=Mazzeo |first2=P. V. |last2=Coveney|title=HemeLB: A high performance parallel lattice-Boltzmann code for large-scale fluid flow in complex geometries|journal=Computer Physics Communications |volume=178 |pages=894–914 |date=2008|issue=12 |doi=10.1016/j.cpc.2008.02.013|bibcode=2008CoPhC.178..894M }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Dynamic endothelial cell rearrangements drive developmental vessel regression|first1=C. A. |last1=Franco |first2=M. L. |last2=Jones |first3=M. O. |last3=Bernabeu |first4=I. |last4=Geudens |first5=T. |last5=Mathivet |first6=A. |last6=Rosa|journal=PLOS Biology |volume=13 |article-number=e1002125 |date=2015|issue=4 |doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.1002125 |pmid=25884288 |pmc=4401640 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Non-canonical Wnt signalling modulates the endothelial shear stress flow sensor in vascular remodelling|first1=C. A. |last1=Franco|first2=M. L. |last2=Jones |first3=M. O. |last3=Bernabeu |first4=A. C. |last4=Vion |first5=P. |last5=Barbacena |first6=J. |last6=Fan|journal=eLife |volume=5 |article-number=e07727 |date=2016|doi=10.7554/eLife.07727 |pmid=26845523 |pmc=4798962 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The algorithm, based on indirect addressing, scales to very large core counts on CPU-based supercomputers. Most recently, he and his team have developed a GPU-accelerated version of the code which scales to around 20,000 GPUs on the [[Summit (supercomputer)|Summit]] supercomputer and will soon{{when?|date=March 2024}} be deployed on the world's first exascale machine, [[Frontier (supercomputer)|Frontier]].<ref>{{cite journal|first1=I. |last1=Zacharoudiou|first2=J. W. S. |last2=McCullough|first3=P. V. |last3=Coveney |title=Development and performance of a HemeLB GPU code for human-scale blood flow simulation|journal=Computer Physics Communications|volume=282|article-number=108548|date=2023|doi=10.1016/j.cpc.2022.108548|arxiv=2202.11770 |bibcode=2023CoPhC.28208548Z |s2cid=246457935 }}</ref>

Coveney works in the domain of multiscale modelling and simulation. Working initially with Eirik Flekkøy on foundations of the dissipative particle dynamics method and then with Rafael Delgado-Buscalioni, he was among the first to develop theoretical schemes which couple [[molecular dynamics]] and continuum fluid dynamics representations of fluids in a single simulation.{{cn|date=March 2024}} His work covers numerous applications of these methods in advanced materials and biomedical domains.<ref name="FCD2000">{{cite journal|first1=E. G. |last1=Flekkøy|first2=P. V. |last2=Coveney|first3=G. |last3=De Fabritiis|title=Foundations of dissipative particle dynamics|journal=Phys. Rev. E |volume=62|pages=2140–2157|date=2000|issue=2 Pt A |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.62.2140 |pmid=11088680 |arxiv=cond-mat/0002174 |bibcode=2000PhRvE..62.2140F |s2cid=46132730 }}</ref><ref name="FC1999">{{cite journal|first1=E. G. |last1=Flekkøy|first2=P. V.|last2=Coveney|title=From molecular dynamics to dissipative particle dynamics|journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=83| page=1775 |date=1999|issue=9 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.83.1775 |arxiv=cond-mat/9908334 |bibcode=1999PhRvL..83.1775F |s2cid=119456909 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Delgado-Buscalioni|first1=R.|last2=Coveney|first2=P. V.|title=Continuum-particle hybrid coupling for mass, momentum, and energy transfers in unsteady fluid flow|journal=Phys. Rev. E|volume=67|article-number=046704|date=2003|issue=4 Pt 2 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.67.046704 |pmid=12786526 |arxiv=cond-mat/0302519 |bibcode=2003PhRvE..67d6704D |s2cid=22997525 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Delgado-Buscalioni|first1=R.|last2=Coveney|first2=P. V.|title=USHER: An algorithm for particle insertion in dense fluids|journal=J. Chem. Phys.|volume=119|pages=978–987|date=2003|issue=2 |doi=10.1063/1.1579475 |arxiv=cond-mat/0303366 |bibcode=2003JChPh.119..978D |s2cid=21241469 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Suter|first1=J.|last2=Groen|first2=D.|first3=P. V.|last3=Coveney|title=Chemically specific multiscale modeling of clay-polymer nanocomposites reveals intercalation dynamics, tactoid self-assembly and emergent materials properties|journal=Advanced Materials|volume=27|pages=966–984|date=2015|issue=6 |doi=10.1002/adma.201403361|pmid=25488829 |pmc=4368376 |bibcode=2015AdM....27..966S }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|first1=J. L.|last1=Suter|first2=R. C.|last2=Sinclair|first3=P. V.|last3=Coveney|title=Principles Governing Control of Aggregation and Dispersion of Graphene and Graphene Oxide in Polymer Melts|journal=Adv. Mater.|article-number=2003213|date=2020|volume=32 |issue=36 |doi=10.1002/adma.202003213|pmid=32720366 |bibcode=2020AdM....3203213S |s2cid=220840677 |url=https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10106755/ }}</ref>

Coveney's recent work is on the rapid, accurate, precise and reliable prediction of free energies of binding of ligands to proteins,<ref>{{cite journal|first1=D.|last1=Wright|first2=B.|last2=Hall|first3=O.|last3=Kenway|first4=S.|last4=Jha|first5=P. V.|last5=Coveney|title=Computing Clinically Relevant Binding Free Energies of HIV-1 Protease Inhibitors|journal=Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation|date=2014|volume=10|issue=3 |pages=1228–1241|doi= 10.1021/ct4007037|pmid=24683369 |pmc=3966525 }}</ref> a major topic in drug discovery. Coveney has noted that classical molecular dynamics is chaotic and to make robust predictions from it requires the use of ensembles at all times.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=P. V.|last1=Coveney|first2=S.|last2=Wan|title=On the calculation of equilibrium thermodynamic properties from molecular dynamics|journal=Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys.|date=2016|volume=18|issue=44 |pages=30236–30240 |doi= 10.1039/C6CP02349E|pmid=27165501 |bibcode=2016PCCP...1830236C |doi-access=free}}</ref> This is a practical manifestation of his earlier work on simpler dynamical systems, for which a thermodynamic description is possible using a probabilistic formulation.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Coveney|first1=P. V.|last2=Penrose|first2=O.|title=On the validity of the Brussels formalism in statistical mechanics|journal=J. Phys. A: Math. Gen.|date=1992|volume=25|issue=19 |page=4947-4966|doi=10.1088/0305-4470/25/19/011|bibcode=1992JPhA...25.4947C }}</ref> It has only become possible in the era of [[Petascale computing|petascale]] computing, when supercomputers have grown to sufficient size to make calculations of ensemble averages feasible.

Working with [[Bruce M. Boghosian]] and Hongyan Wang, Coveney showed that there are a variety of problems which arise when simulating even the simplest of all dynamical systems — the generalised Bernoulli map — on a computer.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=B. M.|last1=Boghosian|first2=P. V.|last2=Coveney|first3=H.|last3=Wang|title=A New Pathology in the Simulation of Chaotic Dynamical Systems on Digital Computers|journal=[[Advanced Theory and Simulations]]|volume=2|article-number=1900125|date=2019|issue=12 |doi=10.1002/adts.201900125|pmid=34527854 |pmc=8427473 }}</ref> The IEEE floating point numbers can produce errors which are extremely large as well others of more modest scale, but they are each wrong when compared with the known exact mathematical description of the dynamics.

In recent years, Coveney has been a leading player in the development and application of validation, verification and [[uncertainty quantification]] (VVUQ) to computer simulation codes across a wide range of domains. The VECAM Toolkit<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.vecma.eu/|title=VECMA}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.vecma-toolkit.eu/|title=VECMA Toolkit}}</ref> and later SEAVEA Toolkit<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.seavea-project.org/seaveatk/|title=SEAVEA Toolkit}}</ref> provide a set of open-source, open-development software components which can be used to instrument any code so as to study its VVUQ characteristics. The methods his team has developed<ref>{{cite journal|first1=P. V.|last1=Coveney|first2=D.|last2=Groen|first3=A. G.|last3= Hoekstra|title=Reliability and reproducibility in computational science: implementing validation, verification and uncertainty quantification in silico|journal=Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A.|volume=379|article-number=20200409|date=2021|issue=2197 | doi=10.1098/rsta.2020.0409|pmid=33775138 |bibcode=2021RSPTA.37900409C |s2cid=232387102 |url=https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/68020393/rsta.2020.0409.pdf }}</ref> are aimed at the analysis of real-world codes of substantial complexity which run on high performance computers.

Coveney has become active in [[quantum computing]], where he is specifically concerned with seeking to assess the feasibility of realising quantum advantage from its application to the solution of molecular electronic structure problems. He and his team are currently dealing with [[noise reduction]] and implementing [[Floating-point error mitigation|error mitigation]] as extensively as possible on a range of quantum device architectures.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=A.|last1=Tranter|first2=S.|last2=Sofia|first3=J.|last3=Seeley|first4=M.|last4=Kaicher|first5=J.|last5=McClean|first6=R|last6=Babbush|first7=P. Coveney led the EPSRC RealityGrid e-Science Pilot Project<ref>{{cite web|url=https://gow.epsrc.ukri.org/NGBOViewGrant.aspx?GrantRef=EP/C536452/1|title=Grants on the web|website=gow.epsrc.ukri.org}}</ref> and its extension project, and the EU FP7 Virtual Physiological Human (VPH) Network of Excellence.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/223920|title=CORDIS &#124; European Commission}}</ref>  He is the Principal Investigator on the EU Horizon 2020 projects Verified Exascale Computing for Multiscale Applications, "VECMA"<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/800925|title=CORDIS &#124; European Commission}}</ref> and Centre of Excellence in Computational Biomedicine,"CompBioMed2".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/823712|title=CORDIS &#124; European Commission}}</ref>  The original CompBioMed initiative<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/675451|title=CORDIS &#124; European Commission}}</ref> was launched after Coveney and his team successfully challenged the EU<ref>{{Cite journal 
| last1 = Callaway | first1 = Ewen 
| doi = 10.1038/nature.2016.19714 
| pmid = 27075075 
| title =  How one lab challenged a grant rejection and won €5 million
| journal = Nature  
| volume = 532
| issue = 7598 
| pages = 159–160 
| year = 2016 
| bibcode = 2016Natur.532..159C| doi-access = free 
}}</ref>  following a rejected grant proposal.

Coveney has been the recipient of US NSF and DoE, and European [[Distributed European Infrastructure for Supercomputing Applications|DEISA]] and PRACE<ref>{{cite web|url=https://prace-ri.eu/wp-content/uploads/Peter-Coveney-Article-2.pdf |title=Article |publisher=prace-ri.eu |date= |access-date=2021-02-13}}</ref> supercomputing awards.

Coveney has chaired the UK Collaborative Computational Projects Steering Panel<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ccp.ac.uk/node/13 |title=About the CCPs &#124; UK Collaborative Computational Projects |publisher=Ccp.ac.uk |date= |access-date=2021-02-13 }}{{Dead link|date=December 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> and served on the programme committee of the 2002 Nobel Symposium on self-organization.<ref>{{Cite journal 
| last1 = Skår | first1 = J. 
| last2 = Coveney | first2 = P. V. 
| title = Self-organization: the quest for the origin and evolution of structure. Proceedings of the 2002 Nobel Symposium on self-organization
| year = 2003}}</ref>  He is a founding member of the UK Government's e-Infrastructure Leadership Council and a Medical Academy Nominated Expert to the UK Prime Minister's Council for Science and Technology<ref>{{cite press release|url=https://www.parliament.uk/documents/lords-committees/science-technology/ScientificInfrastructure/ScientificInfrastructureevidence.pdf |title=Scientific Infrastructure |publisher=www.parliament.uk |date= |access-date=2021-02-13}}</ref> on Data, Algorithms and Modelling, which has led to the creation of the London-based [[Alan Turing Institute]].
